events.title: The Sistine Chapel ceiling unveiled
events.shortBlurb: On All Saints' Day, Michelangelo's newly completed ceiling of the Sistine Chapel was shown for the first time…
body: The chapel of the Apostolic Palace, built for Pope Sixtus IV and consecrated in 1483, received its crowning glory when his nephew Julius II commissioned Michelangelo Buonarroti in 1508 to repaint its ceiling, then a simple field of blue starred with gold.

Working on scaffolding high above the floor for some four years, largely unaided, the artist covered the vault with more than three hundred figures: nine central panels telling the story of Genesis from the creation of light to the drunkenness of Noah, and about them the prophets of Israel and the sibyls of the nations who foretold Christ, with the ancestors of Christ in the spandrels and arches.

The last scaffolding came down on the eve of All Saints in 1512, and on the feast itself, 1 November, Julius II celebrated Mass beneath the finished vault. A generation later Michelangelo returned to paint the Last Judgment above its altar, unveiled in 1541; the chapel still serves the papal liturgies and the conclaves that elect the popes.

events.title: The Lisbon earthquake
events.shortBlurb: A catastrophic earthquake struck Lisbon on All Saints' Day as the churches were full for Mass…
body: At about half past nine on the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day, while the churches of Lisbon were thronged for the feast, the earth shook for several minutes in one of the strongest earthquakes recorded in Europe, its magnitude later estimated at near 8.5.

The shocks brought down churches, palaces, and houses upon the worshippers; a great sea wave swept into the harbor, and fires, fed by the candles of the feast, burned for days. Some eighty-five percent of the city lay in ruins, and between thirty and sixty thousand people perished in Lisbon and the country round about.

The Marquis of Pombal, the king's chief minister, directed the relief and rebuilt the ruined center on a straight grid of earthquake-resistant streets that still stands. Falling on a holy day and levelling the churches with the devout inside them, the disaster provoked a celebrated debate across Europe on providence and evil, answered by Voltaire in his Poem on the Lisbon Disaster of 1756 and again in Candide.

events.title: The dogma of the Assumption defined
events.shortBlurb: Pope Pius XII solemnly defined that Mary, at the end of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heaven…
body: On 1 November 1950, in the midst of the Holy Year, Pope Pius XII, before an immense throng in Saint Peter's Square, solemnly defined the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary as a dogma of the Catholic faith in the apostolic constitution Munificentissimus Deus.

The definition declared it divinely revealed that "the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was assumed body and soul into heavenly glory." The pope had prepared the step in 1946 with the encyclical Deiparae Virginis Mariae, consulting the bishops of the whole world; nearly twelve hundred answered that the doctrine could safely be defined, and only sixteen questioned its opportuneness.

The dogma gathered up a belief attested from the earliest centuries, kept from of old in the feasts of the Dormition in the East and the Assumption in the West, and petitioned by millions of the faithful since the definition of the Immaculate Conception in 1854. It remains the most recent exercise of the solemn papal magisterium, and the feast of 15 August still celebrates what it declared.

sources.text: Apostolic Constitution Munificentissimus Deus, Pope Pius XII (vatican.va)
